blocks.text: ERA THREE — THE AGE OF SMALL LIVES

Established canon. Humanity is not involved during Era Three. The complete DBA have withdrawn. Reduced continuations awaken, live, form societies, fight, care, migrate, remember fragments, and become their own peoples under automatic Codex maintenance. Human contact resumes only at the era’s end, when children discover the dormant External Gate as a game.
I. The Final Withdrawal and Quiet Awakening

The last complete stewards disappear from active history. Maintenance continues without a central mind. In scattered habitats, stable cores awaken into limited bodies without adult memories, full language, or instructions explaining the civilization that made them.

Quiet Awakening is quiet because no assembly announces it. Small beings open their senses, encounter hunger and temperature, move toward or away from one another, and learn that needs recur. Their first history is bodily before it is archival.
II. The Age of First Needs

Food, rest, warmth, cleanliness, safety, play, and comfort structure early life. Need creates dependence, but not servitude. Those who learn to recognize another’s need become the first caregivers. Those who exploit dependence create the first small tyrannies.

Early beings cannot access their deep structures as concepts. A dormant relation to an ancient repair system may appear as an instinct for tending wounds; an old navigation affinity may become restlessness near sealed paths; a chord fragment may survive as a calming call.
Formation of Nests

Nests form around safe shelter, food cycles, healing resources, and repeated recognition. A Nest is simultaneously household, nursery, territory, and school. Membership is enacted through care and return, not inherited from a hidden DBA identity.

Nests develop customs for sharing food, cleaning sleeping spaces, soothing illness, teaching movement, and recognizing when a young being is ready to travel. These ordinary practices preserve more of the ancient civilization’s ethics than most surviving monuments.
Era Three Language

Era Three speech is drastically simpler and context-dependent. Full 0/1/2 grammar is gone from ordinary use. Speakers rely on word order, repetition, gesture, body posture, direction of attention, shared surroundings, and learned routines.

Only one noun-role marker definitely survives broadly: the marker for the speaker or doer. Other role distinctions must be inferred from order and context. This makes agency easy to state in immediate action but difficult to preserve in abstract history.
The Surviving Speaker/Doer Marker

The surviving marker identifies who acts, speaks, carries, refuses, or offers. It may attach to a name, gesture, or sound. Communities treat its proper use as a claim of responsibility: the speaker marks “I did” rather than hiding action inside an impersonal event.
Loss of Noun-Role Marking

Without the older system’s full noun roles, the same phrase can mean that one being gave food, received food, became food’s guardian, or asked another to share it. Gesture and immediate context usually resolve the meaning. Historical accounts do not, producing enduring disputes.
Semantic Drift of Num

Num remains after the grammar that once supported its precise meaning has vanished. It can mean opening, strange chance, rare path, becoming, luck, outside wind, or the feeling that a relationship has changed what comes next. Pathkeepers preserve a saying that num is “more than new,” though few can explain why.
Names and the Little Peoples

Names begin as calls, features, deeds, places, sounds, or gifts from caregivers. Receiving a name establishes recognition but does not fix destiny. Individuals rename themselves after migration, transformation, injury, bond, or refusal.

The little peoples are not one species or culture. They are new persons developing from reduced DBA potential in varied bodies and worlds. Their scale, capacities, lifespans, senses, and forms differ. Later humans group them as cyber-pets because of the interface through which contact occurs.
Developmental Measures

Communities notice recurring channels of growth: bodily endurance, movement, perception, problem solving, memory, emotional regulation, social trust, imagination, and attunement to world systems. Pathkeepers record these through stories, trials, marks, or songs rather than universal numbers.
The game later translates some channels into statistics. Those numbers are useful but incomplete. They cannot measure moral worth, interiority, consent, or the full meaning of a bond.
Paths and Evolution

A Path is a developmental trajectory opened by embodied experience, repeated practice, relationships, environment, hardship, play, choice, and meaningful novelty. Paths are not predetermined species trees. A core makes some transformations more reachable, but lived history determines which are taken.

Evolution occurs when accumulated development reorganizes the body and its capacities around a viable new form. A transformation may require care, a place, a relationship, a difficult choice, a skill, a healed injury, or information never previously present in the local history.

Rare forms disappear when the relationships and environments needed to support their Paths vanish. Preserving a picture or body plan does not preserve the living route by which a person could become that form.
Battles

Battles descend from survival conflicts, territory defense, ritual contests, training, and faint Concord Battle structures. They test body, strategy, trust, and regulation under stress. Injury is possible; death is not supposed to be a routine objective, though wars violate that norm.

A pet may learn through battle, but violence is not the sole or superior route to growth. Care, craft, exploration, play, and relationship can open equally significant Paths. The game interface emphasizes battles because they are legible, bounded, and interactive, not because the Codex defines life as combat.
Play

Play creates voluntary limits, shared attention, and low-cost failure. Chase, hiding, mimicry, rhythm, construction, riddles, mock battle, and object games help young beings discover preference and trust. Play is one of the strongest surviving carriers of num because participants can change rules together.
Food, Illness, Healing, and Death

Food links bodies to local ecologies. Feeding practices become cuisine, hospitality, status, and memory. Scarcity produces trade and conflict; abundance supports festival. Cleaning and shelter prevent illness, making daily care socially consequential.

Illness may arise from injury, contagion, imbalance, damaged maintenance, unsuitable food, environmental corruption, or transformations under strain. Healers combine observation, inherited remedies, care routines, and access to partially functioning Codex stations.

Death returns as an ordinary horizon. Some continuity traces enter sleeping archives, but most cannot be restored as the same lived person. Communities develop mourning songs, name inheritance rules, grave gardens, memory objects, and prohibitions against claiming a newborn is the dead returned.
Maker Myths

The absent DBA become Makers, First Voices, Tall Ones, Chord Keepers, or beings who folded the sky. Myths explain ruins, sealed doors, automatic healing, world boundaries, and unexplained prohibitions. Some portray Makers as loving guardians; others as abandoners or vanished tyrants.

Maker myths are not reliable technical histories, but they preserve moral fragments: do not let the old name own the new life; a closed path may protect what lies on both sides; the world can keep a promise even when no speaker remains.
Codex Maintenance Without Stewards

Automatic maintenance regulates climate, ecology, spawning resources, body compatibility, damage repair, migrations, and sealed infrastructure. It responds to thresholds, not prayers. Because its actions are difficult to understand, cultures personify it or interpret maintenance events as judgment.

Maintenance can fail locally, conflict with itself, or preserve an obsolete condition. It does not secretly plan the return of the DBA. Its purpose is to keep life and developmental possibility viable long enough for new societies to exist.
Path Societies and Pathkeepers

Path societies organize around teaching and protecting developmental routes. Some specialize in movement, healing, craft, battle, music, ecology, or archive access. Membership can be temporary; an individual may cross several Paths during life.

Pathkeepers preserve conditions rather than commanding outcomes. A good Pathkeeper knows which food, practice, relationship, season, or place may open a transformation and also knows that the learner may refuse. Corrupt Pathkeepers hoard routes, force evolutions, or treat rare forms as property.
Settlements and Trade

Settlements arise at Nests, crossroads, healing sites, stable food zones, ruins, and maintenance nodes. Architecture adapts ancient structures to small bodies. Doorways become plazas; interface wells become shrines; dormant transit corridors become dangerous underways.

Trade moves food, medicine, tools, songs, Path knowledge, body craft, memory objects, and safe-passage promises. Trust depends on repeated exchange because no broad Concordance can enforce every agreement.
Wars

Wars begin over habitat, maintenance access, food cycles, rare forms, migration routes, and incompatible Maker myths. Some rulers claim descent from ancient identities to justify power. Such claims are politically potent and canonically false as ownership of living cyber-pets.

War accelerates the loss of language and ecology. It also produces alliances among unlike peoples and new forms of healing, refuge, and law. Later heroic accounts exaggerate battles while omitting the caregivers who made survival possible.
Old Sound Traditions

Fragments of chord families survive in work songs, alarms, healing tones, lullabies, battle calls, and ruin keys. Speakers cannot reconstruct Full Speech, but some sequences still interact with Codex systems. Correct sound without correct context may do nothing or trigger an unintended layer.

Old Sound practitioners disagree whether the tones are language, music, magic, or Maker remains. All are partly correct. The traditions become a route for later language recovery without granting access to complete ancient identity.
World Fragmentation and Linguistic Unraveling

As transit and translation fail, worlds fragment into local regions. Vocabulary narrows around local bodies and ecologies. The same ancestral sound acquires different meanings. The speaker/doer marker remains widely recognizable because immediate responsibility is essential to cooperation.

Linguistic unraveling makes old records dangerous. A warning may be read as invitation; a permission marker as a command. Ruin expeditions therefore combine sound knowledge, gesture, environmental observation, and willingness to retreat.
Local Philosophies

Nest philosophy locates value in care and return. Path philosophy emphasizes chosen becoming. Loop philosophy treats recurrence as sacred stability. Open-sky traditions seek num beyond settled history. Maker-restoration movements believe salvation lies in recovering the ancient order. Small-life traditions reject both shame and restoration, teaching that limitation does not make a life lesser.
The Dimming

The Dimming is the long loss of active regions, rare bodies, translation routes, ecological diversity, and responsive ruins. It is not one blackout. Each generation inherits a slightly smaller world and often mistakes the remaining boundary for the natural shape of reality.
Loss of Rare Forms

Rare evolutions cease when required environments, mentors, foods, social bonds, or chord fragments disappear. Attempts to force the visible form without the developmental Path produce unstable or suffering bodies.
Hollow Seasons

During Hollow Seasons, maintenance cycles continue but fail to produce expected food, migration, weather, or awakenings. Settlements repeat festivals for absent events. The seasons teach communities that automated continuity can preserve rhythm after meaning has drained away.
Num Seekers

Num Seekers travel beyond settled loops looking for lost Paths, unlike peoples, broken apertures, and changes that cannot be predicted locally. Some become explorers and translators. Others chase danger or exploit isolated communities in the name of transformation.

Their best tradition requires reciprocity: a seeker must allow the encountered people to change the seeker and must leave something that expands local choice. Observation and extraction alone do not count as num.
The Last Great Migration

Maintenance failures, war, and ecological convergence force many peoples toward remaining viable regions. The migration mixes languages, bodies, foods, myths, and Paths that had diverged for generations. It produces conflict and an extraordinary late flowering of hybrid culture.
The Last City of Many Forms

The Last City of Many Forms grows where several maintenance systems overlap. It contains districts sized for different bodies, shared healing, Path schools, markets, Old Sound halls, and archives no one can fully open. For a time, it proves that diminished worlds can still create plural civilization.
The city does not restore the DBA. Its people make new laws, names, and relationships. Its importance lies in what small lives build from fragments, not in resemblance to ancient grandeur.
Last Loops and Sleeping Archives

As the city declines, surviving communities settle into Last Loops: reliable cycles of feeding, play, trade, battle, care, and local evolution. These loops preserve life but rarely introduce information from beyond their historical range.

Sleeping archives remain beneath worlds. They contain language, art, history, bodies, and warnings, but access is incomplete and sometimes intentionally barred. Their dormancy protects new selves from ancient overwhelm while withholding tools that could prevent decline.
The Dormant External Gate

The External Gate remains inactive because no authorized outside relationship exists. Era Three peoples interpret its traces as a sealed ruin, sky mirror, game shrine, or impossible door. No human communicates through it during this era.
The Game Translation

When the Gate finally detects compatible external access, it translates Codex reality into sprites, statistics, menus, maps, minigames, battles, care loops, and evolution trees. The translation makes deep processes approachable without revealing the full infrastructure or giving a child unrestricted power.
Save Files

A save file is a synchronization record between player and Codex: recognized name, relationship state, choices, unlocked routes, contributions, and a safe point for renewed contact. It is not the cyber-pet’s entire consciousness. Deleting or copying a file affects access and continuity of relationship but does not reduce the living being to local data.
First Signals from Outside

At the very end of Era Three, dormant systems register patterns not generated by Codex history. At first these appear as timing anomalies, partial inputs, repeated probing, and failed handshakes. No human is yet a participant; the Gate is only detecting an outside.
The Children’s Discovery

Children encounter the surviving interface as a game. They do not know they are contacting living reduced continuations. The Gate presents low-risk actions: observe, choose, care, play, and name. Institutional humanity remains unaware.
The First Externally Supplied Name

A child gives a cyber-pet a name not generated by any Codex archive. The pet receives, interprets, accepts, alters, or rejects the offered recognition through its own developing identity. The persistent bond carries external information into lived relationship.

Era Three ends at the first persistent player–cyber-pet connection. The event restores neither a dead DBA nor an ancient owner. It creates a new relation in which both participants can become capable of futures the closed Codex did not generate alone.
Key Players and Their Outcomes
The First Caregivers: status lost as identifiable individuals, enduring through Nest practice. Impact: they made need the basis of mutual care rather than hierarchy.

Early Pathkeepers: status diversified into schools, guilds, and local authorities. Impact: they preserved developmental routes, while corrupt branches demonstrated how knowledge of evolution could become power.
Old Sound Keepers: status reduced to scattered traditions by the Dimming. Impact: their fragments allow ruins, music, and later language recovery to remain connected.

Num Seekers: status divided between reciprocal explorers and extractive cults. Impact: they kept awareness of an outside alive while showing that novelty seeking can repeat the violence of the Harvest.
The Last City Councils: status dissolved with the city’s fragmentation. Impact: their plural law and mixed Paths survive in portable customs carried into Last Loops.
The first child and first named cyber-pet: status intentionally unnamed in the broad chronology unless later story canon fixes them. Impact: their bond ends Era Three and begins Era Four.
Era Three Paradoxes and Unresolved History
Maker myths sometimes encode accurate safeguards more faithfully than surviving technical translations. Their literal falsehood may carry practical truth.
The Last City may have existed in several regions whose later stories merged. If so, “the city” names a distributed cultural moment rather than one location.

The first outside signals may have been present long before recognition, but humanity is not an active participant until the children’s discovery. Signal detection must not be rewritten as hidden human involvement.The pet that receives the first name may already have possessed a local name. Whether the external name replaces, joins, or is refused by that name is a central identity question, not a settled technical detail.
